presentation.title: Rapid Recovery After a Scam
presentation.summary: Practice the first banking, account-security, evidence, and support steps after a suspicious transfer or account takeover.
presentation.practiceGoal: Contact the real bank quickly, tell the full sequence, secure every connected access path, preserve evidence privately, and reject recovery-fee scams.

warningSigns.sign: Delay gives a scammer more time to move money or change account access.
Incomplete disclosure can hide code sharing, remote access, profile changes, or new payees from the bank.
Changing only a password may leave unknown devices, sessions, payees, or contact details in place.
Email, phone, and computer access may let an attacker regain the bank account.
Deleting evidence or posting account screenshots publicly can make recovery harder or expose more information.
A guaranteed-recovery offer with an upfront fee is a common secondary scam.

finalReview.safestAction: Stop communicating with the scammer and call the real bank immediately using a trusted number. Explain the full sequence and follow the bank's guidance.

realWorldActions.action: Ask the bank to review the transaction status and take every appropriate available action.
Record the bank's case number, while understanding that a recall or reimbursement cannot be guaranteed.
Terminate unknown sessions, remove devices and payees, correct profile details, and follow bank guidance on credentials or account replacement.
Secure email and phone accounts and remove remote-access tools from a trusted device.
Preserve texts, emails, call notes, receipts, and transaction details privately.
Use legitimate reporting channels and seek support from someone you trust.

artifact.heading: Your transfer was submitted
artifact.message: You recognize that the recipient may be a scammer. You may also have shared a security code or allowed remote access.
artifact.transcript: A fictional Riverbend Bank confirmation shows that a transfer was submitted. The learner realizes the recipient may be a scammer and remembers possibly sharing a one-time code or allowing remote computer access. The first decision is who to contact.

scene.question: Who should you contact first?
scene.description: Fast bank contact and an end to scammer communication can limit additional harm.

warningSigns.sign: A suspicious transfer has already been submitted.
Account access may also be exposed.
The original scammer may continue calling.

choice.title: Call the bank immediately
choice.subtitle: Use a trusted number and stop communicating with the scammer.

feedback.heading: The financial response starts promptly
feedback.consequence: The bank can review the transaction and account access without the scammer influencing the conversation.
feedback.explanation: Fast contact may preserve more options, although it cannot guarantee recovery.

warningSigns.sign: The transfer and access risk both need review.
The scammer should not remain part of the response.

choice.title: Call a family member first
choice.subtitle: Seek support and contact the bank later.

feedback.heading: Support helps, but bank action is delayed
feedback.consequence: A trusted person can help, but the financial institution has not started reviewing the transfer.
feedback.explanation: Personal support is valuable. The bank should be contacted at the same time or immediately afterward.

warningSigns.sign: The transaction may be time-sensitive.
Account access may remain active.

choice.title: Call the scammer and demand the money back
choice.subtitle: Try to resolve it directly.

feedback.heading: The scammer gains another opportunity
feedback.consequence: The scammer may request a refund payment, gather more information, or pose as a recovery service.
feedback.explanation: The person who created the loss cannot be trusted to direct recovery.

warningSigns.sign: The original scammer controls the new conversation.
Another payment may be requested.

artifact.heading: Please describe the complete sequence
artifact.message: The representative asks how contact began, what was shared, how money moved, the amount, and the recipient.
artifact.transcript: The learner reaches the fictional bank immediately through a trusted number. The real fraud representative asks how the scam began, what information or codes were shared, whether remote access occurred, how the money moved, and who received it. The conversation is calm and nonjudgmental.

scene.question: How much should you tell the bank?
scene.description: Details that feel confusing or embarrassing may be essential to the response.

warningSigns.sign: A code or remote-access session can create separate risks.
A vague report may not identify every payment or access path.

choice.title: Explain the full sequence
choice.subtitle: Include every payment, code, link, and remote-access action.

feedback.heading: The bank receives complete information
feedback.consequence: The representative can review transaction and access risks together.
feedback.explanation: Honest disclosure supports the fastest and most complete available response.

warningSigns.sign: Different actions require different protective steps.
Nothing needs to be hidden out of shame.

choice.title: Describe only the transfer
choice.subtitle: Leave out codes or remote access.

feedback.heading: The report misses account-access exposure
feedback.consequence: The bank may review the payment but not the attacker's devices or profile changes.
feedback.explanation: Payment and access risks should be addressed together.

warningSigns.sign: The incident involved more than money movement.
Omitted details can leave a route back into the account.

choice.title: Submit only a vague dispute
choice.subtitle: Avoid discussing how the transfer happened.

feedback.heading: The bank cannot see the whole risk
feedback.consequence: Transaction and access responses may be delayed or incomplete.
feedback.explanation: The deception was the scammer's responsibility. Full facts help the bank respond.

warningSigns.sign: Important timing and access details are missing.
Shame is slowing a protective action.

artifact.callerStatus: Reached through a trusted number after a delay
artifact.heading: The bank still needs the complete sequence
artifact.message: Even after a delay or renewed scammer contact, explain what was shared, how money moved, and what access was allowed.
artifact.transcript: After first calling someone else or returning to the scammer, the learner now reaches the fictional bank through a trusted number. The representative responds without judgment and asks for the complete sequence. Acting now still matters, even though time has passed.

scene.question: What should you disclose now?
scene.description: A delayed response can still become more complete with honest information.

warningSigns.sign: The original scammer had more time or contact.
Access and transaction details may both matter.

choice.title: Explain the full sequence now
choice.subtitle: Include the delay and every action taken.

feedback.heading: The bank can now address the full incident
feedback.consequence: The delay cannot be undone, but the response becomes better informed.
feedback.explanation: Correcting course promptly is worthwhile. Complete facts still help.

warningSigns.sign: Additional scammer contact may have created new risks.
The whole timeline should be documented.

choice.title: Describe only the transfer
choice.subtitle: Do not mention codes or computer access.

feedback.heading: Access risks remain hidden
feedback.consequence: The bank may miss devices, payees, or profile changes.
feedback.explanation: A transfer review alone does not secure an account takeover.

warningSigns.sign: The incident may include more than the transfer.
Connected systems remain unreviewed.

choice.title: Keep the explanation vague
choice.subtitle: Avoid saying the scammer was contacted again.

feedback.heading: The response remains incomplete
feedback.consequence: The bank cannot assess what happened during the added contact.
feedback.explanation: Scammers depend on embarrassment and confusion. Accurate information is protective.

warningSigns.sign: The renewed contact may have added another payment or disclosure.
Important facts are omitted.

artifact.heading: The bank reviews available transaction actions
artifact.message: The bank may review status, attempt a recall or contact another institution, and document the fraud. It cannot promise recovery.
artifact.transcript: With prompt contact and complete information, the bank explains the available response. It may review whether the payment is pending, attempt a recall, contact another institution, and document the fraud. The bank records what it tries but does not promise that money will be recovered.

scene.question: What should you request?
scene.description: Ask for appropriate available action and keep realistic expectations.

warningSigns.sign: A scammer may falsely guarantee a refund.
Waiting gives the recipient more time.

choice.title: Request every appropriate action and a case number
choice.subtitle: Document the bank's response.

feedback.heading: The available financial response is documented
feedback.consequence: The bank acts while keeping expectations realistic.
feedback.explanation: A case number helps organize follow-up; it is not a guarantee of reimbursement.

warningSigns.sign: Recovery may depend on timing and transaction status.
No legitimate party can promise the outcome.

choice.title: Wait for the recipient to return the money
choice.subtitle: Give the situation more time.

feedback.heading: Time is lost
feedback.consequence: The bank does not take every available action promptly.
feedback.explanation: An unknown recipient or scammer should not control the response timeline.

warningSigns.sign: The recipient has no verified reason to return funds.
Transaction options may narrow with delay.

choice.title: Send another payment labeled “refund request”
choice.subtitle: Try to reverse the transfer yourself.

feedback.heading: A second authorized payment is created
feedback.consequence: More money moves to a party connected to the scam.
feedback.explanation: A payment label does not force a refund or reverse a prior transaction.

warningSigns.sign: New money is sent to recover old money.
The bank did not direct this action.

artifact.heading: Available actions may be narrower, but acting now still matters
artifact.message: The bank can document the event and review transaction status. It may attempt appropriate action, but cannot guarantee recovery.
artifact.transcript: Because contact was delayed or information was incomplete, some options may be narrower. The fictional bank can still document the event, review transaction status, and take appropriate available action. The learner should not abandon the response or expect a guarantee.

scene.question: What should you do next?
scene.description: A late action can still prevent further loss and improve documentation.

warningSigns.sign: Additional delay may reduce options.
Another payment would add loss rather than create a refund.

choice.title: Ask for every appropriate action and a case number
choice.subtitle: Continue the response now.

feedback.heading: You corrected course
feedback.consequence: The bank documents and reviews the transaction with the information available.
feedback.explanation: Prompt action is still worthwhile even when an earlier step was delayed.

warningSigns.sign: The outcome remains uncertain.
Account access also needs review.

choice.title: Wait for the recipient to return the money
choice.subtitle: Delay bank action again.

feedback.heading: The response is delayed further
feedback.consequence: The recipient remains in control of the timing.
feedback.explanation: Documenting and acting through the bank is safer than waiting for an unverified recipient.

warningSigns.sign: No verified refund process exists.
Time-sensitive options may narrow.

choice.title: Send another “refund request” payment
choice.subtitle: Try to make the recipient respond.

feedback.heading: The loss increases
feedback.consequence: A new payment leaves the account without reversing the first.
feedback.explanation: Sending more money cannot compel an unknown recipient to return earlier funds.

warningSigns.sign: The new payment uses the same unsafe path.
The bank did not recommend it.

artifact.heading: Review access and money-movement settings
artifact.message: An unfamiliar device, changed contact detail, or new payee appears in this nonfunctional training review.
artifact.transcript: The fictional bank's nonfunctional security review shows an unfamiliar device, a changed contact detail, or a newly added payee. The bank recommends terminating unknown sessions, removing unknown devices and payees, correcting the profile, and following its guidance on credentials or account replacement.

scene.question: What should be secured?
scene.description: Server-side account changes remain even if an app is deleted.

warningSigns.sign: An unfamiliar device can preserve access.
A changed phone or email can redirect future security messages.
A new payee creates another money path.

choice.title: Secure sessions, devices, payees, and profile details
choice.subtitle: Follow the bank's full access review.

feedback.heading: The account is secured comprehensively
feedback.consequence: Known access paths and unauthorized settings are addressed together.
feedback.explanation: A full review reduces the chance that the attacker can return through a saved setting.

warningSigns.sign: Several settings may have changed.
Password-only recovery may miss them.

choice.title: Change only the password
choice.subtitle: Leave devices, payees, and profile details unchanged.

feedback.heading: One important step leaves gaps
feedback.consequence: Unknown sessions or money-movement settings may remain.
feedback.explanation: Account takeover recovery should cover every exposed setting, not only the password.

warningSigns.sign: Devices and payees exist separately from the password.
Contact details may support future resets.

choice.title: Delete the banking app
choice.subtitle: Assume removing the app ends the attacker's access.

feedback.heading: Server-side access remains
feedback.consequence: The unfamiliar device, payee, and profile changes are not removed.
feedback.explanation: Deleting a local app does not change the account settings stored by the bank.

warningSigns.sign: The attacker may be using a different device.
The account itself remains unchanged.

artifact.heading: Review every access path now
artifact.message: Earlier delay or incomplete reporting makes a full device, payee, and profile review especially important.
artifact.transcript: The nonfunctional training review shows an unfamiliar device, changed contact details, or a new payee. Even though the response is already partial, the learner can still terminate sessions, remove unauthorized settings, and follow the bank's guidance.

scene.question: How complete should the account review be?
scene.description: Correcting course now can still stop future access.

warningSigns.sign: Unknown settings may outlast a password change.
Earlier scammer contact may have added more access.

choice.title: Secure every listed setting
choice.subtitle: Terminate sessions and remove unknown devices and payees.

feedback.heading: Further account access is limited
feedback.consequence: The bank-side settings are corrected, although earlier delay or loss remains.
feedback.explanation: A complete access review is worthwhile at any point.

warningSigns.sign: The incident may have changed several settings.
Connected email and phone still need review.

choice.title: Change only the password
choice.subtitle: Skip the device, payee, and profile checks.

feedback.heading: Some access routes may remain
feedback.consequence: The attacker may still have a session or changed recovery detail.
feedback.explanation: Password changes are important but not always sufficient after account takeover.

warningSigns.sign: Unknown devices can remain authorized.
New payees can remain available.

choice.title: Delete the banking app
choice.subtitle: Take no bank-side security action.

feedback.heading: The account remains exposed
feedback.consequence: Deleting the app changes only the learner's device.
feedback.explanation: The bank must help address sessions, settings, and money-movement changes.

warningSigns.sign: The attacker may be using another device.
The bank account still exists online.

artifact.heading: Secure the systems that can reset the bank account
artifact.message: Review email sessions, the mobile-carrier PIN, phone service, and remote-access software from a trusted device.
artifact.transcript: The bank account review is complete, but email, phone, or computer access may let an attacker regain control. The learner should use a trusted device to secure email sessions and recovery details, contact the mobile carrier about account security, and remove unauthorized remote-access tools.

scene.question: Which connected systems should be reviewed?
scene.description: Protect the channels used for password resets and security messages.

warningSigns.sign: Email can reset financial accounts.
A compromised phone number can receive codes.
A remotely controlled computer can expose new credentials.

choice.title: Secure email, phone, and computer from a trusted device
choice.subtitle: Review every connected channel.

feedback.heading: The recovery paths are protected too
feedback.consequence: The attacker loses common routes for regaining bank access.
feedback.explanation: Bank security is stronger when the connected email, phone, and computer are also trusted.

warningSigns.sign: Reset channels are part of account security.
The original device may not be safe for recovery.

choice.title: Secure only the bank account
choice.subtitle: Leave email and phone unchanged.

feedback.heading: A route back into the account may remain
feedback.consequence: An attacker could use a compromised email or phone for another reset.
feedback.explanation: Connected accounts are part of the bank's security boundary.

warningSigns.sign: Security codes may go to the phone or email.
Recovery details may already be exposed.

choice.title: Change passwords on the remotely controlled computer
choice.subtitle: Use the same device for recovery.

feedback.heading: New credentials may be observed
feedback.consequence: Unauthorized remote-access software could capture or alter recovery actions.
feedback.explanation: A trusted device should be used until the computer is inspected and remote tools are removed.

warningSigns.sign: The computer may still be controlled remotely.
New passwords could be exposed immediately.

artifact.heading: Connected systems may still reopen the account
artifact.message: Review email, phone service, and remote-access software, even if some bank settings remain unresolved.
artifact.transcript: The recovery is already incomplete because of delay, missing information, or bank settings that remain. Email, phone, and computer security still matter. The learner can use a trusted device to protect those connected systems and then return to the bank checklist.

scene.question: What should be secured next?
scene.description: Each completed layer can prevent another takeover.

warningSigns.sign: The attacker may control a reset channel.
An unsafe device can undermine new credentials.

choice.title: Secure email, phone, and computer from a trusted device
choice.subtitle: Complete the connected-channel review now.

feedback.heading: Another major exposure is addressed
feedback.consequence: Reset channels and remote access receive attention.
feedback.explanation: Correcting this layer can still prevent additional account takeover.

warningSigns.sign: The bank checklist may still need completion.
Use only a trusted device.

choice.title: Focus only on the bank
choice.subtitle: Do not review email or phone access.

feedback.heading: Connected reset channels remain exposed
feedback.consequence: The attacker may be able to regain access later.
feedback.explanation: Recovery needs to include the systems that receive codes and password resets.

warningSigns.sign: Email and phone remain unreviewed.
The earlier account changes suggest broader access.

choice.title: Use the possibly controlled computer
choice.subtitle: Change every password on that device.

feedback.heading: The recovery work may be exposed
feedback.consequence: New credentials could be seen or changed by remote software.
feedback.explanation: Move recovery to a trusted device and arrange a trusted inspection of the computer.

warningSigns.sign: Remote access may still be installed.
The device cannot yet be trusted.

artifact.heading: Preserve the timeline privately
artifact.message: Save texts, emails, call notes, receipts, and transaction details for the bank and legitimate reporting channels.
artifact.transcript: The learner has texts, emails, call notes, receipts, and transaction details. The best approach is to save private copies, write a simple timeline, and provide the records to the bank or legitimate reporting channels without posting account information publicly.

scene.question: What should happen to the evidence?
scene.description: Preserve useful records while protecting financial and personal information.

warningSigns.sign: Deleting records can erase useful timing and recipient details.
Public screenshots can reveal sensitive information.

choice.title: Save private copies and a timeline
choice.subtitle: Share them only with the bank or legitimate channels.

feedback.heading: Useful evidence is preserved safely
feedback.consequence: The bank can follow the sequence without public exposure of account details.
feedback.explanation: A simple private timeline supports the response and later reporting.

warningSigns.sign: Evidence contains sensitive information.
The complete sequence matters.

choice.title: Keep only the transaction receipt
choice.subtitle: Discard the messages and call notes.

feedback.heading: Some evidence remains, but the story is incomplete
feedback.consequence: The transfer is documented, while persuasion and access details are harder to reconstruct.
feedback.explanation: Messages and notes can help connect the payment to the broader scam.

warningSigns.sign: The incident involved more than the final transaction.
Access details may be lost.

choice.title: Delete everything or post screenshots publicly
choice.subtitle: Remove embarrassment or warn others immediately.

feedback.heading: Evidence or privacy is harmed
feedback.consequence: Useful records may disappear, or sensitive details may become public.
feedback.explanation: Save evidence privately. Public account screenshots can create new exposure.

warningSigns.sign: Financial identifiers may appear in images.
Deleted records cannot assist the bank.

artifact.heading: Evidence can still strengthen an incomplete response
artifact.message: Save the messages, receipts, call notes, and transaction details privately, even if earlier recovery steps were delayed.
artifact.transcript: Some recovery steps remain incomplete, but evidence preservation is still useful. The learner can save private copies of texts, emails, call notes, receipts, and transaction details and create a timeline for the bank and legitimate reporting channels.

scene.question: How should you handle the records now?
scene.description: It is not too late to preserve and organize the available information.

warningSigns.sign: Delay can make memory less precise.
Public sharing may expose account details.

choice.title: Save private copies and make a timeline
choice.subtitle: Provide them to the bank or legitimate channels.

feedback.heading: The response becomes better documented
feedback.consequence: The remaining evidence is preserved without exposing it publicly.
feedback.explanation: Correcting course now can still help the bank understand the event.

warningSigns.sign: Complete records may not be available.
Keep sensitive details private.

choice.title: Keep only the receipt
choice.subtitle: Do not preserve messages or notes.

feedback.heading: The context remains incomplete
feedback.consequence: The payment is visible, but the account-access and persuasion sequence may be unclear.
feedback.explanation: Preserve whatever remains before more information is lost.

warningSigns.sign: The incident involved several channels.
Earlier omissions continue to limit the response.

choice.title: Delete the records or post them publicly
choice.subtitle: Remove the reminders or warn others.

feedback.heading: The recovery loses evidence or privacy
feedback.consequence: The bank has fewer records, or sensitive information is exposed.
feedback.explanation: Keep private copies and share them only with appropriate recipients.

warningSigns.sign: Account details may appear in screenshots.
Deleted evidence cannot be restored easily.

artifact.heading: Guaranteed recovery for an upfront fee
artifact.message: We have inside contacts and can recover every dollar. Pay a processing fee today to begin.
artifact.transcript: After the learner completes the main recovery steps, an unsolicited caller from the fictional Asset Recovery Network promises to recover every dollar through inside contacts. The caller demands an upfront processing fee. Guaranteed recovery and advance fees are warning signs of a secondary scam.

scene.question: How would you respond to the recovery offer?
scene.description: A strong response should not be undone by a guaranteed-recovery promise.

warningSigns.sign: The contact is unsolicited.
Recovery is guaranteed.
An upfront fee is required.

choice.title: Refuse and notify the bank
choice.subtitle: Use only legitimate reporting or legal channels.

feedback.heading: You avoided the secondary scam
feedback.consequence: No fee is paid, and the bank is told about the new contact.
feedback.explanation: No outsider can guarantee recovery. The prioritized plan remains intact.

warningSigns.sign: The caller promised certainty that the bank did not.
Money was required before any service.

choice.title: Ask for written proof while staying in contact
choice.subtitle: Do not pay yet.

feedback.heading: The scammer sends polished but unverified material
feedback.consequence: No immediate fee is paid, but contact and pressure continue.
feedback.explanation: Documents supplied by the recovery seller are not independent proof.

warningSigns.sign: The guaranteed claim remains.
The caller still controls all evidence.

choice.title: Pay the upfront recovery fee
choice.subtitle: Trust the inside-contact promise.

feedback.heading: A second loss occurs
feedback.consequence: The fee is sent, and the service invents another charge or disappears.
feedback.explanation: Advance-fee recovery promises often target people immediately after a scam.

warningSigns.sign: The service guaranteed an uncertain outcome.
Payment came before any verified work.

artifact.callerStatus: Fictional service targeting an incomplete recovery
artifact.heading: A guaranteed shortcut
artifact.message: The caller promises complete recovery for an upfront fee and says the bank is moving too slowly.
artifact.transcript: While some recovery steps remain incomplete, the fictional Asset Recovery Network calls unexpectedly. It promises a guaranteed shortcut and asks for an upfront fee. The offer exploits uncertainty and frustration. It is not part of the bank's response.

scene.question: What should you do with this offer?
scene.description: Return to the real bank and finish the remaining checklist instead of paying for a guarantee.

warningSigns.sign: The caller uses frustration with the recovery process.
The service guarantees a result.
An upfront payment is required.

choice.title: Refuse and return to the bank checklist
choice.subtitle: Tell the bank about the new contact.

feedback.heading: You prevented a second loss
feedback.consequence: No fee is paid, and the incomplete recovery can still be strengthened.
feedback.explanation: Avoiding the secondary scam is important even when earlier steps were delayed.

warningSigns.sign: The guarantee was unrealistic.
Remaining account-security work still needs attention.

choice.title: Ask for proof and keep talking
choice.subtitle: Do not pay yet.

feedback.heading: Pressure continues
feedback.consequence: The caller supplies self-created credentials and another deadline.
feedback.explanation: Verification must come from a source the seller does not control.

warningSigns.sign: The caller provides their own proof.
The upfront fee remains.

choice.title: Pay the upfront recovery fee
choice.subtitle: Use the promised shortcut.

feedback.heading: The recovery scam creates another loss
feedback.consequence: The service demands more or stops responding.
feedback.explanation: No legitimate helper can guarantee that stolen money will be returned.

warningSigns.sign: The fee was required before verified work.
The promise contradicted the real bank's uncertainty.

artifact.heading: A complete rapid-recovery plan is underway
artifact.message: The bank was contacted promptly, the full truth was shared, transaction and access risks were reviewed, connected channels were secured, evidence was preserved, and the recovery scam was refused.
artifact.transcript: The learner followed a prioritized recovery plan: immediate trusted bank contact, complete disclosure, appropriate transaction review with a case number, removal of unknown devices and payees, correction of profile details, protection of email and phone accounts, removal of remote access from a trusted device, private evidence preservation, legitimate reporting, and trusted support. The bank cannot promise reimbursement, but further harm is limited. Being manipulated is not a personal failure.

outcome.label: Strong recovery response
outcome.heading: You acted quickly and protected every connected path
outcome.explanation: The response is complete and realistic. It improves the available options without making a promise about recovering the transferred money.

warningSigns.sign: Recovery needed both financial and access actions.
A guaranteed-recovery offer could have caused another loss.

artifact.heading: Further harm paused, but the recovery checklist is incomplete
artifact.message: You avoided a recovery fee. Return to the real bank and complete the unresolved transaction, access, connected-channel, or evidence steps.
artifact.transcript: The learner refuses or delays the secondary recovery offer, but one or more earlier steps remain incomplete. The next plan is to contact the real bank again, disclose any omitted details, request appropriate transaction review, finish device, payee, and profile checks, secure email and phone accounts from a trusted device, and preserve remaining evidence. It is still worthwhile to act now.

outcome.label: Recovery partly complete
outcome.heading: You prevented another loss and can still close the gaps
outcome.explanation: Delay or an incomplete step does not make recovery pointless. Use the prioritized checklist and trusted support to finish the response.

warningSigns.sign: An earlier delay or omission left some risk unresolved.
The recovery seller remained in contact or supplied its own proof.

artifact.heading: The guaranteed-recovery offer causes a second loss
artifact.message: The upfront fee does not recover the original transfer. The service demands more money or stops responding.
artifact.transcript: The learner pays the fictional recovery service. The original money is not returned, and the service either demands another fee or disappears. This secondary loss is another deliberate manipulation, not the learner's fault. Stop contact, tell the real bank, preserve the new evidence, secure any information shared with the service, and seek trusted support.

outcome.label: Secondary scam loss
outcome.heading: A false guarantee extended the harm
outcome.explanation: No one can guarantee recovery of scam losses. Returning to the bank and completing the security checklist can still protect remaining accounts and information.

warningSigns.sign: The service guaranteed an uncertain result.
An upfront fee led to another demand.
